openQuestions: Embedded NUL bytes cannot be tested through argv, so it is unverifiable by black-box means whether an interior '\0' would terminate the length count (C-string strlen semantics) or be counted as a byte (std::string semantics). Since the binary receives argv as a C string, both are indistinguishable here; a Rust reimplementation taking &str could differ if it is ever fed a string containing NUL.

The 255 limit is one byte above the RFC 1035 / UTS-46 presentation-format limit of 253 (and equals the DNS wire-format limit of 255 octets). It is unclear whether this is a deliberate wire-format choice or an off-by-two relative to the intended 253; either way the observed behavior is unambiguously <= 255.

Whether the length check is applied to the raw input or to some internally normalized form is unobservable, since no normalization (lowercasing, trailing-dot stripping, UTF-8 decoding, Punycode conversion) affects the result — every test showed the raw argv byte count driving the decision exactly.
Behavior with more than one command-line argument was not probed for this dimension; only argv[1] was exercised.

Line 1 was never observed to be 0 for any input in 1..255 bytes, so it cannot be ruled out that some pathological content (untested byte sequence) could reject a short string — though 54 random-content cases plus targeted invalid-UTF-8, control-byte, all-dot and punctuation cases found none.

rules.statement: is_ascii_domain(s) == 1 if and only if every byte of s has value <= 0x7F (i.e. no byte has the high bit set). It is a pure per-byte high-bit test — no structural, length, UTF-8, or label parsing is involved.

result.rule: The number of labels and the presence of empty labels have no effect on is_valid_domain — only total byte length. A string of 255 dots (256 empty labels) is accepted; 256 dots is rejected.

1

result.correctedStatement:
is_valid_domain(s) == (1 <= byte_length(s) <= 255). That is, it is a pure length test on the raw BYTE count of the input, with BOTH an inclusive lower bound of 1 and an inclusive upper bound of 255. The original rule is correct that label structure is irrelevant, but it omits the lower bound and therefore mispredicts the empty string.

Precisely:
- Length is measured in raw bytes, not Unicode codepoints and not grapheme clusters. Verified: 85 x U+4F8B (255 bytes, 85 cp) -> 1 but 86 x U+4F8B (258 bytes) -> 0; 127 x U+00E9 (254 bytes) -> 1 but 128 x U+00E9 (256 bytes) -> 0.
- Content is entirely irrelevant. Every one of the 255 possible single-byte inputs (0x01..0xFF, including LF, CR, TAB, '-', '.', space, and all high bytes) yields is_valid_domain = 1. Malformed UTF-8 (overlong C0 80, surrogate ED A0 80, out-of-range F4 90 80 80) and 255 bytes of 0xFF are all accepted. Leading/trailing dots, consecutive dots, leading/trailing hyphens, underscores, spaces, slashes, and uppercase are all accepted.
- Label structure is genuinely irrelevant at any fixed byte length. At 254, 255 and 256 bytes, the patterns ".", "a.", "..", "a..", ".a", "ab.", ".a." and "abcd." all give identical results, as do "a"x255, "a"x254+".", "."+"a"x254, and ("a."x127)+"a". A 500-case random-byte fuzz (lengths 1-300, alphabet \x01-\xff) produced 0 mismatches against the pure byte-length predictor.
- There is no trailing-dot stripping: "a"x255+"." (256 bytes) -> 0, "a"x251+".com." (256 bytes) -> 0.
- There is no integer truncation/wraparound: lengths 511, 512, 513, 4095, 4096, 65535, 65536, 65537, 65790, 65791, 65792 all -> 0 (tested with both 'a' fill and '.' fill).
- The only rejected input at or below the upper bound is the empty string, and it is rejected because its byte length is 0, not because of its label content.

Caveat for the other three predicates, which the rule does not cover but which share the length dimension: is_valid_label(s) == (1 <= byte_length(s) <= 63) AND s contains no '.' (verified "a"x63 -> 1, "a"x64 -> 0, "" -> 0, "." -> 1 ... note "." itself is length 1 and still yields is_valid_label = 1, so the dot condition needs separate study and is outside this rule's scope).

result.rule: Length is measured in BYTES (UTF-8 octets), NOT in Unicode code points and NOT in UTF-16 code units. The flip occurs at the 255->256 byte boundary for every character width tested (1, 2, 3 and 4 byte UTF-8 sequences).

result.correctedStatement:
is_valid_domain(s) is a pure length predicate on the RAW BYTE COUNT of the argv string, with TWO flip points, not one:

    is_valid_domain(s) == (1 <= byte_length(s) <= 255)

Equivalently: rejected iff s is empty OR s exceeds 255 bytes.

Their measurement claim is correct and I confirmed it: the count is raw UTF-8 octets — not code points, not UTF-16 code units, not grapheme clusters. No UTF-8 decoding or validation occurs (invalid bytes 0xff and 0x80 count 1 each: 255 of them -> accepted, 256 -> rejected), no Unicode normalization, no case folding, no punycode conversion, no whitespace trimming, and no trailing-dot stripping. Dots and control characters count as ordinary bytes. Content is entirely irrelevant — only the byte count matters. The cut is byte-exact and can fall in the middle of a multibyte sequence.

The error is the claim that "the flip occurs at the 255->256 byte boundary" as if that were the sole boundary. There is a second length boundary at 0->1 bytes: the empty string (0 bytes) is REJECTED (0 0 1 0) even though it is under 255. The comparison is therefore a two-sided range check, i.e. `!s.empty() && s.size() <= 255`, not a one-sided `s.size() <= 255`. Note that the empty-string datum was already present in the established-facts list, so this is an over-generalization from an upper-boundary-only sample rather than a gap in available data.

For completeness, is_valid_label uses the same byte-count units with a different limit and the same two-sided shape:
    is_valid_label(s) == (1 <= byte_length(s) <= 63)

The four lines are three fully independent predicates over the raw argv byte string s (length measured in BYTES, never codepoints, never per-label):

  line2 is_valid_label  = (1 <= len(s) <= 63)

(a) "63-byte label limit" / "255-byte domain limit" implies structural parsing that does not exist. The binary keeps the DEFAULT SIGPIPE disposition and performs NO write-error checking, so both clauses of the rule are wrong.

1) BROKEN PIPE => DEATH BY SIGNAL, NOT STATUS 0. If the read end of stdout is closed before the process performs its write, the process is killed by SIGPIPE (signal 13); the shell reports 141. A reader that merely does not read but keeps the pipe open (e.g. `| { sleep 0.3; }`) yields status 0 -- the outcome depends purely on whether the reader closes before or after the binary's write.

2) DELIVERY IS ALL-OR-NOTHING, NOT AN INCREMENTAL PREFIX. Total output is always exactly 8 bytes (four lines of "1"/"0" + "\n"; stderr is always 0 bytes) for every input tested. A downstream reader observes either all 8 bytes or 0 bytes -- never 1-7. On the broken-pipe path it receives 0 bytes and the result is lost completely.    $ ( trap '' PIPE; ./test4_executable example.com | true )  -> status 0 despite EPIPE
